div.head: Grið 16
div.ab: ⁊ gyf forworht man friðstol gesece ⁊ þurh þæt feorh geyrne, þonne sy þreora án for his feore, bute man bet gearian wylle: wergyld, ece þeowet, hengenwitnuncg.
And gyf forworht man friðstol gesece and þurh þæt feorh geyrne, þonne sy þreora an for his feore, bute man bet gearian wylle: wergyld, ece þeowet, hengenwitnuncg.

Und wenn ein verwirkter [todesschuldiger] Mensch einen [kirchlichen] Friedenstuhl aufsucht und dadurch das Leben errennt, dann gelte statt seines Lebens (ausser wenn man günstiger begnadigen will) eines der drei [folgenden]: Wergeld, ewige Verknechtung, Gefängnissstrafe.

And if a forfeited [condemned] person seeks a [church] frith-stool and by that runs to safety with his life, then instead of his life (unless one is willing to pardon more favourably) one of the three [following] shall apply: wergild, perpetual slavery, imprisonment.

And if a condemned man seeks sanctuary and thereby saves his life, then unless greater mercy is shown, he is to receive one of three penalties in exchange for his life: wergild, perpetual enslavement, or punishment by hanging in bonds.
div.note: ; AZ: corrected against Rabin p. 26 / 27, October 2026 (was “∅”, now “|”)

seeks sanctuary: This clause employs friðstol as a general term for “sanctuary,” although the word originated as the name for a specific “peace seat” for sanctuary seekers to use when claiming refuge. Such seats were present in the churches at York, Southwell, Hexham, and Beverly, the latter two of which still survive. Notably, York and Beverly are two of the three foundations whose privileges are set forth in the first clause of Northumbrian Church Sanctuary.

punishment by hanging in bonds: The term used here, hengenwitnung, is a hapax legomenon often translated as “imprisonment”; however, the component parts (hengen, “hanging,” and witnung, “torture” or “punishment”) suggest a more severe sentence.
